title: Cross-Platform Inventory Synchronization
business: A retail logistics firm managing inventory across web dashboards and warehouse backend systems.
problem: Runtime errors and data mismatches occur when the web frontend and BEAM-based backend interpret shared inventory data structures differently, leading to inconsistent stock levels.
solution: Gleam provides a unified type system that compiles to both JavaScript for the browser and the BEAM for the server, ensuring shared data models are strictly validated at compile-time on both targets.
steps: Define shared inventory record types in a core Gleam module.
Implement logic for inventory updates using Result types to handle potential failures explicitly.
Compile the core module to JavaScript for the frontend and BEAM bytecode for the backend.
Integrate the generated TypeScript definitions into the web frontend to enforce type safety.
Use pattern matching on the Result type to handle synchronization errors gracefully.
outcome: Developers achieve high confidence in data integrity across platforms, as the compiler prevents mismatched record fields or unhandled error states before deployment.
limitation: The primary trade-off is the overhead of maintaining a shared codebase that must remain compatible with both JavaScript and Erlang runtimes; developers can verify compatibility by running the Gleam compiler for both targets during the CI process.

questions.question: In Cross-Platform Inventory Synchronization, how does Gleam resolve the problem of data mismatches?

By using a runtime exception handler for all inventory updates.
By automatically converting all data to JSON strings.
By relying on the browser to validate backend database schemas.
questions.explanation: Gleam ensures consistency by compiling the same type-safe code to both platforms, preventing mismatches.

questions.question: What is a key limitation of the Cross-Platform Inventory Synchronization approach?
options: The inability to use any external libraries.
The requirement to maintain compatibility across two different runtimes.
The lack of support for Result types.
The inability to compile to JavaScript.
questions.explanation: Maintaining a single codebase that satisfies the constraints of both the BEAM and JavaScript environments is the primary trade-off.
